title: Benedict and the Sunstone's Light
markdown:
Wizard Benedict lived in a tower that clung to the side of Mount Cinder. Shelves sagged under dusty spellbooks. Cauldrons sometimes smelled of burnt toast. His constant companion was Inkpot, a raven with feathers as black as a moonless sky and an uncanny knack for finding Benedict’s always-misplaced spectacles. Benedict was known for carefully sorting his potions, a sock drawer folded with soldier-like neatness, and humming slightly off-key while he brewed.

Today there was no time for sorting. A shimmering scroll arrived on a gust that smelled of pine needles and distant snow: an urgent summons from the Elder of Sunstone Summit. A very important parcel, immediately, and before the moon rose.

Benedict fumbled his spectacles. They had landed on his nose backwards; his breath fogged the lenses. A tremor in his fingers. Chest tight, a knot pulled too snug. He wanted to straighten things, organise things, anything to regain control. The elegant script explained: the parcel was for the Elder himself, so the village of Starfall would have light through the long cold night. Too late, and the great Sunstone, heart of Starfall’s magical lanterns, would dim, plunging the village into gloomy darkness. Not a task for dawdling.

“Right then, Inkpot.” He grabbed a lumpy canvas sack that looked as if it had once held bumpy potatoes. They left the tower’s cozy warmth for a dizzying rope bridge that swayed with every breeze. Below, pine-dark passes wound like sleeping emerald serpents. Cooler air, damp earth, a hidden waterfall. New territory. The wind whispered of shadowed glades, and his stomach did a little flip-flop.

At a crossroads, a ramshackle stall: Griselda the Goblin, wares a jumble of shimmering stones, oddly shaped roots, jars that smelled suspiciously of pickled socks. Beside her, coiled with excellent posture, sat a young dragon no larger than a sheepdog. Cinder, of Mount Cinder’s lower caves, who had impeccable manners and a habit of saying please even to pebbles.

“Ah, Wizard Benedict,” Griselda cackled, dry stones in a tin. “Seeking something of great importance? I have just the thing for a wizard in a hurry. Or perhaps two things.”

Benedict kept his voice steady and asked for a Glow-worm’s Lumina: tiny, elusive, a brilliant steady light, perfect for the Sunstone. Griselda rummaged through an overflowing chest and presented a chipped teacup of violently fizzing purple liquid. Benedict’s shoulders sagged. “That’s fizzy moon-juice, Griselda.” The thought of turning back to tidy the tower was a siren call.

“No, no,” she chirped, pulling out a ridiculously fluffy slipper that looked made from a cloud. “This will keep your feet warm. Much more practical than a tiny bug.”

Cinder cleared a small polite throat. “If I may,” he said, as if declining a second biscuit. “The gentleman asked for light.”

Benedict tried again, describing the Lumina in greater detail. Griselda, mischievous grin, presented a perfectly smooth grey pebble. “This will help you skip.”

The sun was dipping. Shadows stretched. Air colder. He clutched the pebble, knuckles white, precious time wasted. Inkpot, on his shoulder, gave a sharp knowing caw and nudged a small intricately woven basket tucked beneath the overflowing counter. Cinder inclined his head, as if introducing a guest. Benedict peered inside. Nestled in dried moss: a single tiny but undeniably pulsating glow-worm.

Relief. He paid Griselda a much smaller amount than expected, thanked Cinder, who replied “Not at all,” and hurried on, the little basket clutched carefully.

The sky went fiery orange and deep violet. He had to reach the summit before the last sliver of gold vanished. He picked up his pace, sack bouncing. The shortcut: a narrow goat track, treacherous even in daylight. At a steep rocky section a fierce gust tugged his cloak. Loose stones skittered. Rough cliff under an ungloved hand. Acrid ancient air. He hesitated, chest tight again. A particularly loose rock perched above. He knew he had to go down, take the longer safer path. He looked at the Lumina, faint rhythmic light in the dusk. After a moment of doubt he placed the basket in his deepest pocket, secure, and began the slow careful descent, losing irreplaceable minutes with every step. Inkpot’s encouraging chirps from above. Cinder, who had insisted on accompanying them as far as the fork, waited below with the patience of someone who never rushed a queue.

With the last sunlight fading like a whispered secret, Benedict and Inkpot reached the windswept craggy peak. The Elder, wise, eyes like polished amber, stood waiting. Breathless, Benedict presented the glow-worm. She placed it into a small ornate socket on the Great Sunstone. Soft warm light bloomed, golden on their faces, illuminating villagers below. “You have saved Starfall,” she said, a hum like distant bees. “Swiftness. Cleverness. And your companion’s wisdom, no doubt.”

Benedict looked at Inkpot, who ruffled magnificent black feathers. They had not panicked. They had organised what could be organised, and trusted a raven’s nudge when a goblin offered a slipper. The next morning, as the first cheerful rays touched the mountaintops, a small brightly coloured bird fluttered by Benedict’s tower window and chirped a cheerful trilling tune. For a fleeting moment he felt a tiny flicker of the old tightness. Then he remembered the Sunstone’s steady glow, the Elder’s kind amber, Inkpot’s constant presence, and Cinder’s please. He smiled, a true confident smile that reached his eyes, and organised his potion ingredients with a new confident rhythm, humming a tune that was, for once, almost in key. The sock drawer, when he checked it, was already neat. Inkpot found the spectacles on the correct way round, which was how you knew a glow-worm could travel in a pocket and still arrive as light.
characters: Benedict (wizard who sorts potions and socks), Inkpot (a raven who finds misplaced spectacles), Cinder (a young dragon with impeccable manners)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for independent readers
author: StoryGen Community
